questions.title: Enums practice 1
questions.prompt: Which assignment is valid for this enum?
choices: Level level = Level.MEDIUM;
Level level = "MEDIUM";
Level level = 2;
Level level = new Level();
questions.explanation: An enum variable holds one of its declared constants. The constant is reached through the enum type, so Level.MEDIUM is the valid value.

questions.title: Enums practice 2
choices: HIGH
Nothing
questions.explanation: The value is Level.HIGH, so the HIGH case runs and prints the text 3. The other cases are skipped.

questions.title: Trace Enums
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The variable can hold one Status constant. Java checks the name during compilation. The resulting output is 'ACTIVE'.

questions.title: Enums practice 5
questions.prompt: Why does `Status status = Status.ACTIVE;` catch mistakes that `String status = "active";` does not?
choices: A misspelled enum constant is a compile error, but a misspelled string is not
Enums use less memory than strings
Strings cannot be compared with equals()
Enums are automatically saved to a file
questions.explanation: `Status.ACTIVns` would not compile, so a typo is caught before the program runs. `"actvie"` is a perfectly valid string, so the same typo slips through and fails silently later. The benefit is compile-time checking and a clear type, not memory or storage.

questions.title: Enum valueOf input
questions.prompt: Why can `Status.valueOf(text)` fail for user input such as `"active"`?
choices: `Status.valueOf(text)` requires an exact constant name. Input such as `"active"` does not match `ACTIVE` unless you clean or convert it first.
Represent a fixed set of choices as arbitrary strings.
Assume `valueOf` accepts any capitalization.
Add new enum meanings only in scattered if statements.
questions.explanation: `valueOf` expects the exact enum constant name, including capitalization. User text often needs trimming, case conversion, validation, or a friendlier lookup path before it is converted to an enum.

questions.title: Fixed choices
questions.prompt: When is an enum a good fit?
choices: Store an enum as text when type checking would help.
Use an enum for a fixed set of choices.
Compare user input directly to enum constants without cleaning it.
Use an enum for values that users can invent freely.
questions.explanation: An enum is right when the allowed values are a fixed named set, such as `ACTIVE`, `PAUSED`, and `CLOSED`. The compiler can then help prevent misspellings that loose strings would allow.

questions.title: Clear constants
questions.prompt: What makes enum constants easier to use across a project?
choices: Duplicate the same allowed choices in several files.
Depend on ordinal numbers for permanent saved meaning.
Name constants clearly and consistently.
Use a boolean when there are more than two named states.
questions.explanation: Clear, consistent constant names give the whole codebase one spelling for each state. That beats copying string literals or relying on ordinal numbers whose meaning can drift when constants are reordered.

questions.title: Store enum values
questions.prompt: Why store an enum value instead of a matching string when the state is known?
choices: Forget to handle a new enum constant in branch logic.
Treat enum names as display text for every user.
Parse text without handling invalid input.
Store the enum value instead of a matching string.
questions.explanation: An enum variable can only hold one of the declared constants, so invalid states are harder to represent. A string can carry typos and unexpected casing until much later in the program.

questions.title: Cleaning outside text
questions.prompt: What should happen before outside text is passed to `valueOf`?
choices: Handle outside text before calling `valueOf`.
Use magic numbers instead of named constants.
Let each caller invent its own spelling for a state.
Switch on strings when enum constants exist.
questions.explanation: Outside text should be normalized or checked so the program can handle bad input deliberately. Calling `valueOf` directly on raw text turns ordinary user variation into an exception path.

questions.title: Switching on enums
questions.prompt: When does a `switch` over enum constants make sense?
choices: Put unrelated states into the same enum.
Use switch when each constant needs different behavior.
Assume enum constants are lowercase strings.
Use an enum to store changing numeric data.
questions.explanation: A switch is useful when each named enum constant needs different behavior. The enum keeps the set of possible cases finite, and the branch code can focus on what each state means.
